♻ ☆ Few-shot Classification as Multi-instance Verification: Effective Backbone-agnostic Transfer across Domains
Xin Xu, Eibe Frank, Geoffrey Holmes
We investigate cross-domain few-shot learning under the constraint that fine-tuning of backbones (i.e., feature extractors) is impossible or infeasible---a scenario that is increasingly common in practical use cases---and show how representing few-shot classification as a series of multiple instance verification (MIV) tasks enables competitive classification performance using the static embeddings produced by frozen, "black-box" backbones. More specifically, based on this novel representation, we introduce a new approach to few-shot domain adaptation named the "MIV-head": a classification head that is backbone-agnostic and computationally efficient. We show that the core components of the MIV-head, when trained on few-shot data from a target domain, collectively yield strong performance on test data from that domain. Importantly, they do so without fine-tuning the backbone, requiring only the "meta-testing" phase. In experiments under various settings on an extension of the Meta-Dataset benchmark for cross-domain few-shot image classification, using representative off-the-shelf convolutional neural network and vision transformer backbones pretrained on ImageNet1K, we demonstrate that the MIV-head achieves highly competitive accuracy when compared to state-of-the-art "adapter" (or "partial fine-tuning") methods applied to the same backbones, while incurring substantially lower adaptation cost. Moreover, compared to our approach, well-known "classification head" approaches achieve a substantially lower level of accuracy. We share our code at: https://github.com/xxweka/MIV-head.

♻ ☆ POI Recommendation with LLM-Augmented Multi-Graph Learning and Contrastive Alignment
Burak Tamer, Wolfram Höpken, Zehui Wang, Thomas Bayer
Point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models based on graph neural networks achieve strong performance by propagating collaborative signals over user-item interactions, yet they struggle with the cold-start problem, where items with few or no interactions are not represented. In this paper, we propose LLM-augmented Multi-Graph Contrastive Learning (LLM-MGCL), a multi-graph neural network that uses semantic and spatial information about items to extend the LightGCN backbone with two auxiliary item-item graphs: a semantic graph constructed from sentence embeddings of LLM-generated photo summaries and keywords, and a geographic graph derived from Haversine distances between business locations. Item embeddings are propagated over all three graphs in parallel, fused additively, and aligned across views through a bidirectional InfoNCE contrastive objective that connects behavioral, semantic, and spatial representations of the same items. Experiments on the Yelp Multimodal Recommendation Dataset show that LLM-MGCL outperforms classical collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, and non-contrastive graph neural network baselines. It improves Recall@20 by 48.5% and NDCG@20 by 59.0% over LightGCN, while trailing the strongest contrastive baseline, Self-supervised Graph Learning (SGL), slightly in aggregate. A popularity-stratified evaluation shows that LLM-MGCL achieves the highest recall on cold and warm items, whereas SGL remains better on popular items. An ablation study reveals that the cross-view contrastive alignment (CA) is the primary driver of the aggregate gains. Our results suggest that externally grounded, LLM-derived item knowledge can partially compensate for missing collaborative signal and mitigate the item cold-start problem in POI recommendation.
♻ ☆ Meta-learning of Gibbs states for many-body Hamiltonians with applications to Quantum Boltzmann Machines
Ruchira V Bhat, Rahul Bhowmick, Avinash Singh, Krishna Kumar Sabapathy
The preparation of quantum Gibbs states is a fundamental challenge in quantum computing, essential for applications ranging from modeling open quantum systems to quantum machine learning. Building on the Meta-Variational Quantum Eigensolver framework proposed by Cervera-Lierta et al. and a problem-driven ansatz design, we introduce two meta-learning algorithms: Meta-Variational Quantum Thermalizer (Meta-VQT) and Neural Network Meta-VQT (NN-Meta VQT) for efficient thermal state preparation of parametrized Hamiltonians on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Meta-VQT utilizes a fully quantum ansatz, while NN Meta-VQT integrates a quantum--classical hybrid architecture. Both use collective optimization over a finite set of training parameter values to prepare approximate Gibbs states at held-out parameter values within the sampled parameter domain. We validate our methods on Transverse Field Ising Models (TFIM) with up to eight qubits and on a two-qubit Heisenberg model with all field terms. Within these finite-size benchmarks, the trained models accurately prepare thermal states at test points inside the training interval. For the six and eight qubit cases of TFIM, meta-learned parameters when combined with appropriately designed ansatz serve as warm-start initializations, significantly outperforming random initializations in the optimization tasks. Furthermore, a 3 qubit Kitaev ring example showcases our algorithm's effectiveness across finite-temperature crossover regimes. Finally, we apply our algorithms to train a Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM) on a 2-qubit Heisenberg model with all field terms, achieving enhanced training efficiency, improved Gibbs state accuracy, and a 30-fold runtime speedup over existing techniques such as variational quantum imaginary time (VarQITE)-based QBM highlighting the practicality of meta-algorithm-based QBMs.

♻ ☆ DashVMC: Real-Time Discrete World Model Control in Geometry Dash NeurIPS 2026
Florent Tariolle, Florian Yger
World-model agents are usually evaluated in simulators that can wait for the policy; live games impose the opposite constraint, requiring capture, prediction, and action before the next frame. We present DashVMC, which learns a compact, action-conditioned world model from approximately two hours of recorded Geometry Dash gameplay. To test whether the learned dynamics are actionable, a controller is initialized by behavioural cloning (BC) and refined with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) entirely in frozen-model rollouts, without further interaction with the live game. Across three controller seeds, the refined policies survive longer than their BC initializations on all three official levels and a held-out community layout. At deployment, the baseline skips visual generation and sustains a 60-Hz capture-to-action loop on a consumer GPU. Action-conditioned continuations and rollout diagnostics show that the model remains useful for control despite imperfect long-horizon fidelity.

♻ ☆ Exact and Asymptotically Complete Robust Verifications of Neural Networks via Ising Solvers
Wenxin Li, Wenchao Liu, Anzhe Jiang, Weihao Li, Chuan Wang, Qi Gao, Yin Ma, Hai Wei, Kai Wen
We present an Ising-compatible framework for formal neural-network robustness verification under bounded input perturbations. For piecewise activations (both continuous piecewise-linear and discrete piecewise-constant), the Exact Logarithmic Piecewise Model (Log-PW) provides an exact, sound, and complete formulation with a state-optimal logarithmic encoding, reducing the binary variables per neuron from linear $O(κ)$ to information-theoretically minimal logarithmic complexity $O(\lceil \log_2 κ\rceil)$ via logarithmic SOS2 (Log-PWL) and SOS1 (Log-PWC) constraints. For general element-wise activations, the Asymptotic Step-Envelope Model (Step-Env) leverages Log-PWC to construct sound, refinable endpoint enclosures. An exact monotonic reduction based on Jordan decomposition further extends this framework to arbitrary non-monotonic activations. ☆ Cambium: Participant-Built Commitment Roots for Shared Digital Infrastructure
Mansoor "Manny" Ahmed, Dann Toliver, Ekaterina Pavlova
Commitment services, such as timestamping, transparency logs and provenance registries, let a party prove that it bound itself to a record without publishing the record. Today an operator runs them, or a blockchain replaces the operator at the cost of network-wide agreement on every write. We present Cambium, a permissioned peer-to-peer service in which participants build each cycle's commitment root together, so that no single party decides which inputs the root includes. Fixed-size committees certify inputs and use a recursive-doubling merge, in which disjoint groups recompute every intermediate value, to spread root construction across all participants. A successful cycle costs each node $O(c\log(n/c))$ messages for committee size $c$, and each node stores its own $O(\log(n/c))$ proof per cycle, along with the $O(n)$ membership roster. A Go prototype on AWS with $c=4$, 8-256 nodes and simulated stragglers completes cycles in 12-148 ms and verifies proofs in under 1.5 ms, and demonstrates logarithmic growth. We show that conflicting certificates identify their signers, that a proof binds a signed input to its root, and that two conflicting roots both become final only if at least a third of the nodes are Byzantine, except with probability exponentially small in the number of committees. We also set out the membership, proof-availability and exclusion questions a community deploying Cambium must answer.

However, the substitution is imperfect: when inclusion safety rests on the replicas' connectivity, it requires a longer epoch compared to when the client is well connected.

A single parameter, the number of queries in a tile, now sets the vector length of every part of the kernel and can be matched to the machine. Both reductions also disappear. The second moves the polynomial's coefficients into scalar registers, removing the spills and cutting the softmax's vector memory instructions by 78.7%. On silicon the two together cut whole-kernel cycles by 1.84 to 2.08x at a head dimension of 64, raising floating-point utilization from 16.2% to 29.7% of peak. An FPGA of the same design ranks the changes identically and scores them higher, at 2.71x.

♻ ☆ Quantifying and Defending against the Privacy Risk in Logit-based Federated Learning
Sheng Wan, Dashan Gao, Hanlin Gu, Lixin Fan, Daning Hu, Qiang Yang
Federated learning aims to protect data privacy by collaboratively learning a model without sharing private data among clients. Unlike traditional parameter-based FL methods that exchange model weights or gradients during training, emerging logit-based FL approaches share model outputs (logits) on public data. This strategy promotes model heterogeneity, reduces communication overhead, and enhances clients' privacy. However, the potential privacy risks associated with these logit-based methods have been largely overlooked. This research presents the first theoretical and empirical analysis of a hidden privacy risk in logit-based FL methods - the risk that a semi-honest server (adversary) may learn clients' private models from logits. To quantify and address this threat, we develop the Adaptive Model Stealing Attack (AdaMSA) by leveraging historical logits during training. Notably, we observe that this inherent privacy risk persists even when public data is unrelated to private data, emphasizing the urgency to address privacy vulnerabilities in logit-based FL methods. Moreover, our theoretical analysis establishes the bounds of this privacy risk. We then propose a simple but effective defense strategy that perturbs the transmitted logits in the direction that minimizes the privacy risk while maximally preserving the training performance. We further provide a theoretical analysis of FedLP's privacy and utility properties. The experimental results validate our analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of AdaMSA and our defense strategy.

Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.

♻ ☆ NanoCP: Taming Load Imbalance in Data-Expert Parallel Decoding under Variable-Length Workloads ASPLOS 2027

Modern serving systems for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models adopt hybrid data-expert parallelism: expert parallelism (EP) shards experts across GPUs to scale capacity, while data parallelism (DP) replicates attention layers across instances to process independent requests. Existing systems bind each request's attention, MoE communication, and KV cache to a single instance. Because attention latency scales with KV cache size while MoE communication latency scales with batch size, this binding cannot balance both simultaneously, producing EP stragglers; it also fragments KV memory across instances, inflating tail latency under long contexts. While existing context parallelism (CP) mitigates these constraints, existing group-level and uniform CP designs incur prohibitive communication and attention-side overheads. We present NanoCP, which decouples MoE communication from KV cache placement and achieves dual balance through dynamic context parallelism (DCP). DCP assigns each request a context-parallel degree sized to its KV footprint: long requests distribute attention across multiple instances; short requests remain local. This dynamic parallelism effectively liquefies the KV cache across DP instances within each node, balancing both the per-instance KV cache occupancy and batch sizes without unnecessary load-balancing costs. To bridge DCP with static execution, NanoCP introduces an ahead-of-time (AOT) graph engine paired with a custom routing-based communication backend. Experimental results show that, under 99% TPOT-SLO attainment, NanoCP achieves $3.27\times$ and $2.11\times$ the maximum sustainable request rate of the best-performing vLLM baseline on the DeepSeek-V3 Issue 1% and Issue 5% workloads, respectively, while reducing P99 TPOT by $1.94\times$ and $2.01\times$ on the same two workloads, respectively.

For long-running applications that require frequent reconfiguration due to changes in resource allocation, partitioning, or task placement, this design choice presents a core trade-off between adaptability and performance. Co-locating state with computation ensures low latency at steady state but makes reconfiguration disruptive, as any change forces state migration. On the other hand, keeping state in an external store makes reconfiguration seamless, but incurs overhead on every access. To achieve that, it employs a lightweight ownership transfer mechanism that safely decouples event routing from state location. We implement Koala in a new streaming dataflow system and evaluate it on real-world and synthetic benchmarks. When compared with the state-of-the-art protocol DRRS, Koala consumes backlog up to 23x faster and transfers 8.7x less state on average during reconfiguration.

Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+nτ+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $τ$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.

☆ The Token-Energy Law of LLM Decode: Active Bytes and Realized Time Account for Joules per Token

Energy-efficient deployment of large language models requires understanding how model architecture, hardware, and serving settings shape energy per generated token. We introduce the Token-Energy Law, a compact, interpretable model of GPU-board energy per output token for dense, full-history decoding. It relates token energy to two core dimensions: active bytes and realized decode time. Active bytes describe logical byte demand per output, separating dense weights shared within a decode iteration from private key--value (KV) histories read and updated for each request. Realized decode time is the elapsed decode duration divided by the number of output tokens produced. We combine the two byte coordinates and time in a common affine form, with coefficients calibrated for each model and hardware/runtime configuration. This formulation explains how batching amortizes shared-weight work, longer attended histories increase private KV demand, and throughput determines the time-associated cost per output. Decentralised federated learning (DFL) trains personalised models on devices that average with their neighbours rather than with a central server. Real devices, however, are often offline for hours or days, and a client returning from an outage can recover only by aggregating the models its neighbourhood holds. We observe that the stalest of these models is usually the client's own, a case that existing staleness-aware rules, which discount only the models a client receives, do not address. We formalise aggregation after an outage as estimating the state of a fully available network and derive three principles. First, the receiver must be discounted like any neighbour. Every rule that weights it at least as much as each neighbour has an error that grows without bound with the outage, whereas discounting all candidates by relative staleness keeps the error bounded. Second, staleness must be measured as inherited lag rather than age, since local training resets a model's age but not the lag it absorbed from stale neighbours. We introduce the effective lag, which tracks this quantity at the cost of one scalar per message. Third, the discount must be steep, because absorbed lag persists in every later round. These principles define Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip (SFG), a family of drop-in aggregation rules with the communication and computation of decentralised federated averaging, whose guarantees hold for the stale receiver itself. On three image benchmarks and eight outage processes, including real smartphone availability traces, the lag-based members SFG-L and SFG-Cut consistently outperform decentralised federated averaging and recent age-of-information rules, and ablations show that each principle is necessary. The analysis also explains why tuned limited merging from gossip learning is effective.

The resulting encoder and decoder can be implemented using smoothing splines with linear master-side complexity. We derive a non-asymptotic bound on the worst-case end-to-end approximation error by decomposing it into three components: (1) the encoder approximation error, (2) the decoder reconstruction error under fully honest results, and (3) the adversarial perturbation error. For maximum of $q\geq 1$ adversarial workers among $N$ workers results in a worst-case error of order $\mathcal{O}((q/N)^{6/5})$ with appropriate selection of smoothness parameter, demonstrating that the approximation error vanishes asymptotically whenever the number of adversaries grows sublinearly with the network size. Experiments on scalar computation and neural-network inference are consistent with the predicted convergence behavior.
♻ ☆ Carbon-aware Resource Management for Latency-Sensitive Cloud Computing Environments: A Taxonomy and Future Directions
Tharindu B. Hewage, Shashikant Ilager, Maria Rodriguez Read, Rajkumar Buyya
The proliferation of cloud-based latency-sensitive workloads, such as autonomous driving, real-time healthcare services, industrial automation, immersive interactive services, and intelligent AI-based applications requires infrastructures tuned to meet stringent latency constraints. Today, these workloads are reshaping the cloud from a general-purpose computing platform into a diverse ecosystem of workload-specific cloud environments. As demand for latency-sensitive workloads grows, cloud providers must scale their infrastructures accordingly, adversely increasing the carbon footprint and challenging net-zero goals. However, the strict performance requirements and rigid deployment patterns used to satisfy latency Service Level Objectives (SLOs) constrains conventional carbon optimization. Therefore, novel carbon-aware techniques are needed to exploit application-specific opportunities for reducing both operational and embodied carbon footprints while preserving latency guarantees. This survey examines carbon-aware resource management for latency-sensitive cloud computing environments. We introduce a holistic taxonomy that organizes existing techniques by carbon management objective, workload management mechanism, control architecture, system tier, latency requirements, and deployment stage. Then, we use this taxonomy to classify and critically analyze existing approaches, revealing the interactions and trade-offs between latency guarantees and operational and embodied carbon reduction. Finally, we identify limitations in the literature and present a structured research agenda for the design of sustainable latency-sensitive cloud systems.
♻ ☆ SeFoRA: Sketch-Aggregated Federated Low-Rank Adaptation with Heterogeneous Client Ranks
Yue Xia, Tayyebeh Jahani-Nezhad, Mayank Bakshi, Rawad Bitar
We consider federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning of foundation models, e.g., LLMs and LVMs, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA; ~Hu et al.\ 2022). Combining LoRA with federated learning introduces challenges absent from either setting alone: clients may use different LoRA ranks, making their factor matrices dimension-incompatible, and factor-wise averaging suffers from a bilinear mismatch. We propose SeFoRA, a sketch-aggregated federated LoRA algorithm in which each client transmits a linear sketch of its local $Δ\mathbf{W}$ updates, enabling direct aggregation at the federator. As a result, SeFoRA overcomes the rank heterogeneity challenge and alleviates the bilinear mismatch. We establish convergence to a neighborhood of a first-order stationary point at rate $\\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$. Extensive numerical experiments on language and vision models showcase the performance of our algorithm compared to existing methods.
♻ ☆ Dooly: Configuration-Agnostic, Redundancy-Aware Profiling for LLM Inference Simulation
Joon Ha Kim, Geon-Woo Kim, Anoop Rachakonda, Daehyeok Kim
Selecting the optimal LLM inference configuration requires evaluation across hardware, serving engines, attention backends, and model architectures, since no single choice performs best across all workloads. Profile-based simulators are the standard tool, yet they hardcode their operation set to a specific configuration and re-profile every operation from scratch, making exploration prohibitively expensive. This cost stems from a missing structural understanding: every input dimension of each operation is fixed by the model configuration or determined by the incoming request. Many model-configuration values (e.g., head size, layer count) recur across models, so the same operation runs in many configurations; a single sweep over the request-dependent dimensions can serve them all. We present Dooly, which exploits this structure to achieve configuration-agnostic, redundancy-aware profiling. Dooly performs a single inference pass, labels each input dimension with its origin via taint propagation, and selectively profiles only operations absent from its latency database; stateful operations such as attention are isolated by reusing the serving engine's own initialization code, eliminating manual instrumentation. From this database, it builds latency regression models that serve as a drop-in backend for existing simulators. Across two GPU platforms, three attention backends, and diverse model architectures, Dooly achieves simulation accuracy within 5% MAPE for TTFT and 8% for TPOT while reducing profiling GPU-hours across 12 models by 56.4% compared to the existing profiling approach. We have open-sourced Dooly at https://dooly-project.github.io.
♻ ☆ FEAST: Federated Shared-Space Training for Resource-Heterogeneous Clients
Bostan Khan, Masoud Daneshtalab
Federated learning (FL) must serve devices with varying computational capabilities. A fixed model cannot suit all devices, while training one model per deployment limit is costly. Federated supernet training instead learns one elastic model with differently sized subnetworks, then deploys a suitable one to each device. When client inference budgets differ, however, parameters exclusive to high-cost subnetworks are reachable by fewer clients. We propose FEAST, a federated shared-space training framework that counters this imbalance by jointly training multiple subnetworks within each client's limit. Budget-tailored sub-supernet routing sends only the relevant supernet portion, and sparse aggregation merges the returned parameter slices. The trained supernet directly serves the subnetworks used during federation and supports post-hoc extraction of additional subnetworks without federated retraining. We further show that independently assigning clients' training-data volumes and inference budgets can distort accuracy--inference-cost comparisons in heterogeneous FL simulations, and introduce a one-parameter $γ$-allocation protocol to control this coupling. In our experimental setup, the SuperFedNAS and DeepFedNAS supernet training procedures remain near chance at 25M and reach at most $17.09\%$ at $596$M inference MACs; FEAST reaches $71.06\%$ at $596$M, $2.4$ points above the strongest model-heterogeneous weight-sharing baseline at its largest tier. Across CIFAR-100, CINIC-10, and TinyImageNet-200, FEAST achieves the highest population-averaged accuracy among the evaluated weight-sharing methods when each client receives its largest affordable subnetwork. Sub-supernet routing reduces aggregate model-parameter traffic by $6.8\times$ relative to full-supernet transmission.

♻ ☆ QwenGyre: An Elastic Reinforcement Learning Framework for Training xLong-Horizon Agents
Weiqi Wang, Yuxin Zhou, Mouxiang Chen, Siyuan Zhang, Yi Zhang, Yuyan Luo, Zhiyu Yin, Chencan Wu, Jiemin Jiang, Wentao Yao, Chujie Zheng, JianWei Zhang
Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly undertake extreme-long (xlong) horizon tasks, where a single execution can span hours, hundreds of model--environment interactions, and nearly 1M tokens per rollout. Applying online reinforcement learning (RL) to such executions poses two fundamental challenges: (1) severe execution variance and prolonged rollout delays cause massive GPU idling; and (2) complex non-linear branching generates massive trajectory redundancy, crippling training efficiency. To address these, we presents QwenGyre, an end-to-end framework for xlong-horizon online RL. QwenGyre elastically reallocates GPUs between rollout and training without interrupting live executions, while its trajectory processor reconstructs branching histories, scores partial progress, and deduplicates redundant paths to bound training costs. Scaled to our flagship model, Qwen~3.8 2.4T, with 700K tokens per rollout, QwenGyre yields a 6.0% absolute gain on NL2RepoBench (52.5% $\to$ 58.5%) in 48 steps. Across our evaluations on diverse domains of training datasets, QwenGyre delivers up to $1.85\times$ and $1.78\times$ speedups over Colocate and Async, respectively.
♻ ☆ Online Continual Learning on Intel Loihi 2 via a Co-designed Spiking Neural Network
Elvin Hajizada, Danielle Rager, Timothy Shea, Leobardo Campos-Macias, Andreas Wild, Eyke Hüllermeier, Yulia Sandamirskaya, Mike Davies
Edge AI must adapt to new classes and shifting data within a tight power budget, but online continual learning (learning from each sample before the next arrives) is where conventional processors are least efficient: each small update pays a full dispatch at full power. We present CLP-SNN, a spiking architecture that recasts the Continually Learning Prototypes (CLP) algorithm as event-driven neural dynamics: a self-normalizing local rule replaces CLP's global renormalization, prototype allocation becomes novelty-triggered neurogenesis, and correctness-modulated plasticity becomes reward-gated per-neuron metaplasticity. Deployed on Intel Loihi 2 as the first online continual learner on that chip, rehearsal-free CLP-SNN matches Replay and SLDA on OpenLORIS at 1-shot; at 25-shot, it stays within 0.8 percentage points of Replay and 6.2 points below covariance-based SLDA. Each prediction-and-update step on extracted features completes on-chip in 0.33 ms at 0.05 mJ, 7.3x lower latency and 341x lower energy than Replay on a Jetson Orin Nano.
♻ ☆ NVIDIA Spectrum-X: Hardware-Accelerated Multiplane Networking for Large-Scale AI Training
Sajy Khashab, Albert Gran Alcoz, Alon Gal, Jacky Romano, Rani Abboud, Yonatan Piasetzky, Lior Maman, Amit Nishry, Barak Gafni, Omer Shabtai, Matty Kadosh, Dror Goldenberg, Gilad Shainer, Mark Silberstein
As distributed model training scales to span hundreds of thousands of GPUs, scale-out networks face unprecedented performance and efficiency demands. NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet has been designed from the ground up to achieve predictable and stable network performance with high utilization and low latency. This paper presents the Spectrum-X multiplane architecture, which replaces hierarchical depth with topological parallelism, and introduces hardware-accelerated load balancing in NICs and switches as the key architectural approach to provide fast reaction to highly dynamic network conditions at the microsecond timescales that AI training workloads demand. We describe the motivation, design principles, evaluation methodology and performance on state-of-the-art benchmarks, as well as the lessons we learned from deploying and debugging Spectrum-X networks in large-scale systems. Our evaluation highlights production-grade AI infrastructure performance across four core dimensions: 98% of the theoretical line rate with low jitter-free latency; strong cross-tenant isolation for concurrent workloads; robust, capacity-proportional bisection bandwidth and 7% latency increase for 10% fabric link failures; and rapid reaction to host and fabric link flaps during LLM training workloads.
♻ ☆ OpenAgenet / OAN Yellow Paper: Technical Architecture for Trust-Governed Resource Identity and Discovery
Jinliang Xu
This yellow paper describes the technical architecture of OpenAgenet / OAN. OAN is a protocol-neutral trust layer for open Agent interconnection and discoverable AI resource products. It specifies the role architecture, did:oan identity objects, registration workflow, governance-backed Root lifecycle enforcement, Root-verified package model, authorization-aware Discovery, Root-issued infrastructure authorization VCs, signed trusted invocation, Root's trust, data-distribution, and semantic-governance hub responsibilities, verification requirements, state transitions, security properties, implementation boundaries, and deployment considerations. The design is intended to support heterogeneous Agent frameworks and interaction protocols, including MCP, A2A, ANP-like systems, domain-specific Agent protocols, Skills, MCP Servers, and Tool/API resources. OAN does not define the entire business conversation among Agents or the native protocol of every resource; it defines how resource identities become admissible, discoverable, verifiable, and safe to approach before protocol-specific interaction begins, and how defined profiles carry that identity into protected protocol interaction.
♻ ☆ DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
Bin Ma, Min Yu, Vijay Kodamalla, Jonny Liu, Da Li, Dong Li
On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.

☆ SweepANN: A GPU-Accelerated Large-K Approximate Vector Search for Drug Discovery
Zhenyu Zhang, Qi Lin, Nan Zhang, Zhichao Cao
DrugCLIP places small molecules and protein pockets in one space, turning genome-wide drug discovery into large-K retrieval by vector proximity. A campaign fixes over 20K pockets in advance for one library of over 500M molecules. Each pocket keeps K = 500K candidates, 0.1% of the collection, versus 100 in ANN benchmarks. Missed hits never get tested, so mean recall must reach 99% relative to exact search. Large answers make IVF probe every list holding a result and graph search track K or more candidates, so costs grow with K. On our CPUs and GPUs, neither index family reaches the target without losing most of its edge over scanning. SweepANN partitions compressed vectors across GPUs and scans each resident partition. One matrix multiplication scores each block for a whole query batch, reading it once. Several plans perform the K-dependent selection and merging of each query's K answers, each returning an exact top-K under compressed scoring. The window plan retains each query's best K from sampled blocks as its seed, and only rows above each seed's minimum score, shared once across GPUs, enter the buffers. Four Blackwell GPUs (RTX PRO 6000) answer all 26,562 pockets with a resident time of about 61 seconds, excluding library loading, and 99.6% mean recall relative to exact FP32 search. DrugCLIP reports roughly 24 hours with eight A100 GPUs in its own campaign. On 500M rows, the window plan runs 1.41x faster than SweepANN's grouped plan in the same memory. Across 25M-500M rows and K of 10K-500K, all GPU IVF configurations meeting the recall target take 8.2-24x SweepANN's resident time. On DEEP1B's 1B vectors across eight GPUs, against SweepANN's exact full-score scan of uncompressed FP32 rows, the window plan cuts resident time by 5.4x and 3.2x at K = 100K and 500K. It also cuts per-GPU peak memory by 6.0x and 5.3x, losing 1.0 and 0.7 mean-recall points.

☆ FaaSpot: Fault-Tolerant Serverless Workflow Execution on Spot Instances
Bandhan Patel, Sushruth Harsha, Kwangsung Oh, In Kee Kim
Serverless computing is increasingly used to run complex DAG workflows across diverse applications, and individual function execution times have grown to support them, pushing workflow makespans to hours. Open-source serverless platforms, deployed on a pool of VMs, typically use on-demand instances, and their cost increases with the makespan. Spot instances are far cheaper, but a preemption is likely before the workflow finishes. A preemption at a fan-out node or a task feeding a fan-in node stalls every parallel branch, cascading a single preemption into a workflow-wide failure. Prior systems address this challenge by migrating high-impact tasks to reliable, non-spot resources, sacrificing spot's cost advantage. We present FaaSpot, a serverless workflow execution system that runs every workflow task on spot instances with no on-demand fallback. Our key insight is that cascade-prone positions are determined by the DAG's topology and can be identified before execution. Therefore, FaaSpot analyzes the workflow DAG once at submission time and classifies each task by the impact of its preemption. Selective checkpointing, survival-aware scaling, and lineage-based retry then act on this single classification, with no runtime coordination. We evaluate FaaSpot on a trace-driven spot emulator with eight DAG workflows against four state-of-the-art baselines. FaaSpot completes 89.03% of runs at $0.018 per successful run, 21pp (percentage points) above the average baseline success rate and at a lower cost per success than every baseline, while reducing mean latency by 2.3x.

☆ GeoSplit: Selective Edge--Server Map Acquisition for Cross-User Travel-Mode Recognition
Zepu Wang, Luyao Niu, Ruolin Li, Jeff, Ban
Networked mobility sensing couples local trajectory inference with remote geospatial context, making communication decisions part of the prediction system. We present GeoSplit, an edge--server framework for travel-mode recognition that separates the utility of map evidence, its training-time transfer, and its selective acquisition at runtime. On GeoLife with 10% labels, we evaluate these components under user-day and user-disjoint grouping. For unseen users, aligned full-map context raises macro-F1 from 0.7154 to 0.7864, while map-informed distillation yields a motion-only student at 0.7225. Through a compact query interface, entropy gating achieves 0.7729 macro-F1 versus 0.7738 for all queries, querying 39.5% of trajectories and reducing application payload by 60.5%. Under user-day grouping, selective and all-query scores are similarly close at a 21.6% query rate. Learned value estimation and probability fusion offer no consistent improvement. These results illustrate communication-efficient edge--server inference for an intelligent transportation sensing task.
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
☆ CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers SC26
Kanglin Xu, Yash Kurkure, Yihe Zhang, Michael E. Papka, Zhiling Lan
HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet much of this operational data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into actionable insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. CQTwin addresses this gap through two complementary modes: offline trace replay and online event-driven simulation. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab, enabling facility staff, operators, and researchers to characterize workloads, compare scheduling policies, and explore what-if scenarios. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies to show how the same workload would have unfolded under different scheduling decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, providing guidance for real-time decision-making. The dashboard supports the complete analysis workflow, including workload characterization, experiment configuration and monitoring, and multidimensional comparison of simulation results, allowing users to determine visually which policies best suit a workload and what trade-offs they entail. We validate CQTwin using production traces from the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility spanning 2016-2023.

☆ SafeWall: A Risk-Aware Job Walltime Recommendation for HPC Scheduling SP
Kanglin Xu, Michael Papka, Zhiling Lan
In high-performance computing (HPC), users must submit resource requirements for their jobs, with user-supplied walltime being a critical parameter. However, these estimates are notoriously inaccurate, as users tend to overestimate walltime to prevent the scheduler from terminating their jobs prematurely. While existing work on learning-based walltime prediction primarily focuses on maximizing prediction accuracy, such predictions are inherently risky for walltime recommendations. Specifically, underestimation leads to job termination before completion, resulting in lost progress and wasted resources. In this study, we present SafeWall, a novel recommendation method that adjusts walltime predictions by incorporating an explicit, nonnegative safety buffer to mitigate underestimation risk. The core of our approach is a risk-aware buffer that dynamically calibrates safety margins based on individual user's historical behavior. When user data is limited, the system employs statistical shrinkage to align these margins with a global baseline, ensuring robustness. This yields a lightweight mechanism that optimizes the trade-off between prediction accuracy and termination risk. SafeWall is modular and applicable to various learning-based prediction models. We evaluate SafeWall using five public workload traces, including the full-lifetime job log from the 4,392-node Theta machine at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility. Across all traces, SafeWall substantially reduces underestimation risk compared to the unbuffered base predictors, while preserving competitive accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SPEAR-UIC/JSSPP26-SafeWall.
comment: Accepted at the 29th Workshop on Job Scheduling Strategies for Parallel Processing (JSSPP 2026), held with IEEE IPDPS 2026. 20 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables
☆ KrMM Recurrences: HPC-Enhanced Estimators for Nonlinear Classical Shadows
Matthias Gruber, Sabrina Herbst, Ivona Brandic, Vincenzo De Maio
While quantum technologies are rapidly evolving, near-term applications heavily rely on hybrid quantum-classical paradigms. Among these, the classical shadows framework has gained a lot of traction, not only for quantum information science, but also for the development and verification of quantum hardware. It allows to efficiently classically estimate many properties of quantum states from randomized measurements alone, a task that is otherwise intractable due to the destructive nature of measurements in quantum systems. There are, however, many properties of interest that are, due to their very problem formulation, not efficiently estimable. In this work, we identify a computational kernel occurring in estimators of polynomial functions, a class of problems that are in general computationally difficult to solve. We show that this structure allows a row-wise partition that, together with a custom SIMD vectorization, enables massive parallelization and can reduce the computational cost significantly. We show applicability and scalability of the approach on different tasks, and our results showcase that the approach allows high sequential throughput and close-to-ideal parallel scaling. The work thus provides a new way of identifying and exploiting structure in classical shadow estimators, resulting in practical advantages on inherently difficult problems.
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures
☆ A Generic On-Board AI Processing Chain for Earth Observation: From Application Development to Embedded Deployment and Mission-Level Orchestration
Michel-Fran{\c c}ois Foulon, Liz Ramos Medina, Thomas Goudemant, Clotilde Szywala, Virgile Robles, Cl{é}ment Petitjean, Ad{è}le Hankache, Omar Hlimi
Earth observation satellites acquire more data than they can downlink. Extracting information on board with artificial intelligence (AI) turns the satellite into a data-reduction stage that downlinks compact products, such as masks or detections, instead of full scenes; deploying it in a mission, however, involves the whole processing chain and not only the neural network. We present a generic on-board AI processing chain along three axes, with wildfire segmentation as the worked example among ship detection and cloud segmentation. (i) The AI model is tuned (spectral-band selection, input normalization), quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an AMD Versal VCK190, with its excellent segmentation performance preserved on the board. (ii) A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow, reused unchanged across applications, brings the tile-level model to scene level, turning a full acquisition into a scene-level mask or detection list. (iii) Each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by ORCHIDE, a cloud-native orchestrator. The chain is characterized end to end, from the standalone execution on the target to its execution under orchestration with parallel workflows on a representative test bench. Beyond AI inference on individual tiles, this approach aims at increasing the maturity of on-board AI deployment by addressing a complete processing chain, from the acquired scene to the mission-level execution.
☆ Pangolin: Efficient DAG-based BFT State-Machine Replication with TEE-Accelerated Commitment
Paul Franke-Bergmann, Maya Kuhlmann, Alexander Heß, Marc Leinweber, Rüdiger Kapitza, Hannes Hartenstein, Franz J. Hauck, Christian Berger
Currently many Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) protocols use directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to let replicas propose blocks of requests in parallel for improved throughput. Yet, the existing DAG-based designs mainly consider the atomic-broadcast layer: They typically do not describe an efficient client interaction layer, their garbage collection is either unspecified or relies on trusted external storage, and the lowest-latency designs rely on timing assumptions that may be violated in geo-distributed deployments. In this paper, we propose the Pangolin protocol: It introduces a novel low-latency DAG-based atomic broadcast layer and completes it into an efficient state-machine replication (SMR) framework. To preserve system throughput, clients issue requests to a single replica and verify replies efficiently via compact execution proofs. Furthermore, Pangolin introduces a new garbage-collection scheme for DAGs which bounds memory usage even under full asynchrony. Pangolin leverages trusted execution environments to tolerate f Byzantine faults with only n >= 2f + 1 replicas and accelerates vertex commitments significantly: Broadcasting certified vertices requires only a single communication step, and commit rules are refined to commit both frequently and early without revealing the coin-elected anchor. This way, Pangolin overtakes the fastest partially synchronous DAG protocols while being live under asynchrony: In our evaluation, Pangolin achieves an average 1.27x (up to 1.52x) latency speedup over Mysticeti.
comment: 28 pages
☆ Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
Masashi Aono
On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.

☆ Bridging In-Situ Visualization to Game Engines: From ParaView Catalyst via ANARI to Unreal Engine SC26
Thomas George, Severin A. T. Klapproth, Jens Henrik Göbbert, Jonathan Windgassen, Andreas Adelmann, Sriramkrishnan Muralikrishnan
In-situ high-performance computing (HPC) simulations produce massive datasets that remain difficult to stream into game engines for interactive visualization. We present an in-situ, disk-free pipeline that couples simulation data to Unreal Engine 5 through ParaView's ANARI rendering API. A modified ANARI-USD device captures Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graphs in memory at the ANARI layer and streams the engine-agnostic USD format through an embedded ZeroMQ broker to visualization clients, where JuSync, middleware with a companion Unreal Engine 5 plugin, parses the geometry as it arrives and routes it to engine rendering components at runtime, producing scenes that are camera-navigable once received. The decoupled design keeps simulation execution independent of visualization load, and clients may connect or disconnect at any time. The pipeline is demonstrated on the JURECA-DC supercomputer at Forschungszentrum Jülich, streaming Free Electron Laser (FEL) simulation data with point clouds of tens of millions of particles.

☆ GeoTrain: Energy-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Foundation Model Training on Heterogeneous Geo-Distributed Resources
Bui-Khanh Hoang, TianZhang He, Mohammad Goudarzi
Training foundation models at the frontier typically requires large-scale dedicated and centralized clusters with fast interconnects - infrastructure that is prohibitively expensive and generally accessible only to well-resourced organizations. Decentralized training over pooled, geographically distributed GPUs offers an alternative, but introduces substantial heterogeneity in compute, memory, power, and network performance. Existing distributed training systems are primarily designed for clusters with fast, low-latency interconnects and typically use all available GPUs when configuring parallel training. In geo-distributed environments, however, slower devices and weak network links can become bottlenecks, while optimizing solely for throughput overlooks significant energy cost. We present GeoTrain, an automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes training performance and energy consumption for heterogeneous geo-distributed GPU environments. GeoTrain simultaneously selects GPUs, partitions model layers, and determines pipeline configurations while accounting for heterogeneous compute, memory, power, and network constraints. To efficiently explore this large combinatorial search space, GeoTrain employs an optimized memetic algorithm with specialized genetic operators and local search. Experiments with decoder-only Transformer models on real-world and simulated heterogeneous topologies demonstrate that GeoTrain reduces iteration time and energy consumption by up to $61.4\%$ and $11.7\%$, respectively, over the existing state-of-the-art approaches. It also finds the exact optimum on verifiable instances and scales beyond exact methods as the number of GPUs increases, while exposing favorable energy-time trade-offs, including cases where its time-optimal distributed training plan is both faster and more energy-efficient than the baselines.
☆ CEMA-Router: Infrastructure-Aware Batch Routing for LLM Inference in Cloud-Edge Systems
Xijia Wang, TianZhang He, Mohammad Goudarzi
Large language models (LLM) are increasingly integrated into pervasive applications spanning heterogeneous cloud-edge resources. These heterogeneous resources differ in computational capacity, energy efficiency, network conditions, and deployed model quality, creating trade-offs among response quality, monetary cost, energy consumption, and batch completion time when routing inference requests. Existing LLM routers typically make per-query routing decisions based primarily on model quality and token cost, whereas cloud-edge schedulers often overlook quality differences among deployed models. Consequently, these objectives remain insufficiently coordinated. We present CEMA-Router, an infrastructure-aware batch router for LLM inference in pervasive cloud-edge systems. CEMA-Router formulates batch routing as a multi-objective search problem that jointly minimizes model-quality loss, monetary cost, energy consumption, and straggler-dominated batch completion time. To efficiently explore the search space, it employs a routing-specific memetic algorithm, combining largest-request-first, load-aware seeding with probabilistic, evaluator-guided Lamarckian repair. Routing decisions are informed by deployment-specific node profiles, dynamic backlog estimates, and model-quality signals. We further implement CEMA-Router as an end-to-end system comprising a request manager, routing service, and profiler, supporting both real cloud-edge deployment and trace-driven simulation. We evaluate the system using RouterBench traces and GSM8K and MMLU workloads on a heterogeneous cloud-edge testbed. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, CEMA-Router reduces the weighted objective by up to 86% for GSM8K and 80% for MMLU, while reducing energy consumption by up to 33% and 19% and batch completion time by up to 27% and 30%, respectively.

Existing resource management approaches often rely on static resource requirements or prior workload profiling, limiting their ability to respond to changing resource contention as required in the cloud. In this paper, we leverage workload buoyancy, a runtime framework for capturing workload sensitivity to individual resources and application-level performance, to enable adaptive scheduling and resource management. We propose a holistic approach that incorporates buoyancy into workload scheduling, node-local resource allocation, and workload rescheduling throughout the workload lifecycle. We implement our approach as a Kubernetes-native prototype and evaluate it on a multi-node cluster using diverse cloud workloads under varying levels of resource contention. In a high-congestion scenario, our approach increases the percentage of workloads satisfying their SLOs from 7.74% to 87.8% on average compared with the Kubernetes baseline, while reducing resource congestion, the severity of SLO violations, and cluster fragmentation using limited rescheduling.

☆ Fault-Tolerant Offloading Framework for Real-Time Applications in Mobile Edge Computing
Chuanchao Gao, Yiyang Gao, Michael Yuhas, Arvind Easwaran
This paper studies a Deadline-constrained task Offloading and resource Allocation Problem (DOAP) in a backhaul-network-enabled Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) system with both bandwidth and computational resource constraints. The goal is to maximize the total inference accuracy improvement across all tasks. We formulate this problem, denoted as $\mathbf{P}$, as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem and show it is NP-hard via a reduction from the maximum-weight three-dimensional matching problem. To address $\mathbf{P}$, we develop $\mathtt{FastSA}$, a linear-time $\frac{1}{10}$-approximation algorithm based on the local-ratio technique. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathtt{FastSA}$ provides the first constant-factor performance guarantee for backhaul-network-enabled DOAPs. In addition, we introduce a fault detection and recovery framework that enables robust MEC operation under backhaul link and edge server failures. Experiments using profiled image classification workloads and real-world taxi traces show that $\mathtt{FastSA}$ achieves an average accuracy improvement of $25.6\%$ over benchmark algorithms under fault-free conditions while maintaining the lowest runtime. Under fault-injected scenarios, our framework reduces performance degradation by an average of $12.8\%$, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault handling.
☆ An Event-Driven System Architecture for a 15-Minute Urban Flood Digital Twin: A Hanoi Case Study
Mai Anh Tran, Vy Nguyen, Vova Nguyen
Flash floods in Hanoi submerge roads within minutes of heavy rain onset, yet public flood advisories remain retrospective. Hydrodynamic models could supply forward-looking depth guidance, but they are typically run offline for historical events, and prior studies have not evaluated whether physics-based simulation, spatial serving, and vehicle-aware routing can operate together within a fixed refresh cycle using a cloud solver and a single commodity server. This paper evaluates an end-to-end prototype of an automated flood digital twin designed to meet a 15-minute refresh cycle under data scarcity. The architecture organizes execution into decoupled, event-driven workflows that chain weather-gated 3Di simulations through hydraulic restart states, serve flood depths through a dual-track spatial layer, and publish road-edge depths via standardized output contracts. Evaluated on a 57-run storm replay in the My Dinh and Tay Mo sector of Hanoi driven by satellite rainfall estimates, every cycle completed within the 15-minute deadline, publishing a ready edge table at a median of 537 s after slot start. Indexed raster tiles resolved point-depth lookups in a median of 0.54 ms (277 times faster than un-tiled rasters), while pre-rendered vector tiles served web maps without database queries. These findings demonstrate that a commodity server coupled to a cloud solver can sustain the 15-minute operational cycle and decouple routing policies from simulation internals. Because simulated depths were not validated against field gauges and the replay used observed satellite rainfall, the results establish system feasibility rather than forecast accuracy or route safety.
☆ 3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Hardware-Software Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP
Yudong Pan, Lian Liu, Shixin Zhao, Yintao He, Kaiyan Chang, Tianhua Han, Chenyang Ai, Haonan Zhu, Mengdi Wang, Yinhe Han, Ying Wang
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) have become a mainstream way to scale Large Language Models (LLMs), because each token activates only a small subset of experts, reducing inference cost. However, MoE decode remains highly memory-bound and exhibits strongly skewed, time-varying expert loads. 3D-stacked DRAM near-memory processing (NMP) provides the bandwidth that decode demands, yet its tiled organization makes load balancing expensive: expert parallelism (EP) preserves locality but suffers from hotspot-induced imbalance, while more distributed strategies weaken locality and increase NoC traffic. To address this locality-balance conflict, we observe that domain-specialized token routing creates offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps, a property we call expert complementarity. Using this insight, we propose 3D-MoE, a hardware--software co-designed system for MoE decode on 3D-stacked NMP. 3D-MoE uses offline, one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping to establish coarse-grained inter-group balance, handles residual intra-group hotspots through a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) that streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path, and uses cost-aware online remapping to remain robust to workload drift. Across MoE models, 3D-MoE achieves an average 4.63$\times$ MoE-layer speedup over EP and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.58$\times$--1.86$\times$ over the strongest NMP baselines, with 2.11\% additional logic-die area.

Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Building on our earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submis-sions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.

♻ ☆ LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas
Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
♻ ☆ HyCo: Hybrid Drafting for Cost-Efficient Mobile-Cloud Speculative Decoding ACL
Hanbin Bae, Heejin Choi, Joohyung Lee, Byoung Jin Choi, Sangjun Park, Hoon-Young Cho
Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which runs the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head on the device to build a deep chain and uses one SLM pass to add alternative branches. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An ε-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three runs of each system on Spec-Bench show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-ε. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.

♻ ☆ Fault Tolerance for Stream Processing Engines
Muhammad Anis Uddin Nasir
Distributed Stream Processing Engines (DSPEs) target applications related to continuous computation, online machine learning and real-time query processing. DSPEs operate on high volume of data by applying lightweight operations on real-time and continuous streams. Such systems require clusters of hundreds of machines for their deployment. Streaming applications come with various requirements, i.e., low-latency, high throughput, scalability and high availability. In this survey, we study the fault tolerance problem for DSPEs. We discuss fault tolerance techniques that are used in stream processing engines that were state of the art at the time of writing (2016), namely S4, Storm, Flink, Spark Streaming, Samza and MillWheel. Further, we give insight on fault tolerance approaches that we categorize as active replication, passive replication and upstream backup. Finally, we discuss implications of the fault tolerance techniques for different streaming application requirements. This revised version corrects errors in the original 2016 manuscript, summarizes later developments in Flink and Spark, discusses durable logs and archival storage for replay, and points to more recent surveys.

♻ ☆ Magneton: Optimizing Energy Efficiency of ML Systems via Differential Energy Debugging
Yi Pan, Wenbo Qian, Dedong Xie, Ruiyan Hu, Yigong Hu, Baris Kasikci
The training and deployment of machine learning (ML) models have become extremely energy-intensive. While existing optimization efforts focus primarily on hardware energy efficiency, a significant but overlooked source of inefficiency is software energy waste caused by poor software design. This often includes redundant or poorly designed operations that consume more energy without improving performance. These inefficiencies arise in widely used ML frameworks and applications, yet developers often lack the visibility and tools to detect and diagnose them. We propose differential energy debugging, a novel approach that leverages the observation that competing ML systems often implement similar functionality with vastly different energy consumption. Building on this insight, we design and implement Magneton, an energy profiler that compares energy consumption between similar ML systems at the operator level and automatically pinpoints code regions and configuration choices responsible for excessive energy use. Applied to 9 popular ML systems spanning LLM inference, general ML frameworks, and image generation, Magneton detects and diagnoses 16 known cases of software energy inefficiency and further discovers 8 previously unknown cases, 7 of which have been confirmed by developers.

♻ ☆ Democratizing MoE inference on commodity GPUs with CoMoE
Ruwen Fan, Yuezhi Zu, Minhui Xie, Junru Li, Qingda Hu, Xinjun, Yang, Jiwu Shu, Youyou Lu
Deploying Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models relies heavily on Expert Parallelism, which generates intense inter-GPU communication. Consequently, state-of-the-art inference systems require high-bandwidth, P2P interconnects (e.g., NVLink) in datacenter GPUs to handle massive token routing, making deployment prohibitively expensive. Consumer GPUs offer comparable compute power at significantly lower cost, promising to democratize MoE inference for individuals and enable privacy-preserving local deployments. However, their bandwidth-limited (only weak PCIe bus bandwidth) and host-mediated interconnects (no P2P support) introduce severe communication bottlenecks. We present CoMoE, a communication-efficient MoE inference system that resolves this mismatch through novel host-centric routing. Our key insight is that the unique communication topology provides the opportunity to elevate the host to an active routing hub, which can fundamentally reduce communication volume and eliminate global synchronization-induced stalls. Specifically, for token dispatch, we introduce host-backed token multicast to write shared tokens to the host exactly once, eliminating outbound transmission redundancy. For token combine, we propose a fine-grained, token-level aggregation mechanism using host staging buffers, which replaces rigid global synchronization and mitigates straggler effects. Evaluation on RTX 5090 GPUs shows that CoMoE improves inference throughput by up to 1.46x, approaching the performance of NVLink-capable A800 GPUs at only 23.4% of the hardware cost.
♻ ☆ Thread Scaling of Hexaly on the TDVRPTW across Two Model Encodings. An Experimental Report: Binding Choice, Slice-Count Choice, and Two Thread Ladders
Florian Rascoussier
Thread scaling in Hexaly on the Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (TDVRPTW) depends on modeling, and on the language binding through which the model reaches the solver. We compare two encodings, both reaching the solver through its C++ binding: one evaluates continuous travel-time functions exactly through external callbacks, which that binding evaluates concurrently, while the other approximates them with time slices evaluated natively by the solver. Independent CPU accounting confirms that both use the cores they are allocated, but they respond differently to width. The external-function encoding stabilizes, reducing its seed dispersion by about 30% up to 8 threads before widening again, yet its pooled quality barely moves, because nine of the ten instances improve while the hardest one degrades by enough to cancel them. For the time-sliced encoding we first select a discretization on feasibility under the original travel-time functions rather than on approximation error, and the retained setting then improves monotonically with the thread count, gaining about a quarter of its final gap and reducing the seed dispersion by nearly half between 1 and 16 threads. At equal single-threaded budget the two encodings are close, and the small pooled edge of exact evaluation comes from that same hardest instance, so the practical advantage of the discretization is thread scaling rather than fidelity traded for speed. These descriptive results support multi-threading as a way to improve solution quality and stability when the model can exploit it, and they show that binding-level constraints on external evaluation must be measured, not assumed.

♻ ☆ Dynamic Load Balancing for Uncertainty Quantification with Applications in Bayesian Inversion
C. M. Loi, M. Wille, A. Reinarz
Uncertainty quantification (UQ) workflows present a particular scheduling challenge in high performance computing environments, as they typically generate large numbers of heterogeneous model evaluations with loose but non-trivial dependencies between tasks. A static one-size-fits-all approach in traditional schedulers is inadequate to handle heterogeneous tasks optimally. We introduce an improved load balancer in the UQ and Modelling Bridge (UM-Bridge) framework aimed at mitigating these issues; UM-Bridge is a language-agnostic interface developed to couple UQ software with numerical simulation. This load balancer is first benchmarked against the previous implementation using a synthetic problem. Then, as a realistic example, we test the load balancer with a Bayesian inverse problem solved via multilevel delayed acceptance sampling. The underlying forward problem is a hierarchy of tsunami simulations enabled through ExaHyPE, whose runtimes span several orders of magnitude and loose dependencies between levels make the workload particularly challenging to schedule. Our results indicate the load balancer distributes the sampling requests effectively with an average idle time of close to a millisecond, a thousand times lower than the previous version, without any prior assumptions about the workload or application.
♻ ☆ Memory Profiling and Migration for Heterogeneous Memory Architectures
Marios Asiminakis, Polydoros Petrakis, Manolis Marazakis
Heterogeneous memory systems that combine high-bandwidth memory (HBM) with commodity DRAM can accelerate bandwidth-bound HPC workloads, but current page placement largely depends on manual tuning or OS heuristics not designed for multi-tier dynamics. We present SHAMBLES, a kernel-integrated framework that profiles application memory behavior at low overhead and migrates data across tiers without requiring application changes. SHAMBLES exposes a policy-agnostic interface and a lightweight user-space runtime with pluggable policies (e.g. recency and frequency based) as well as static placement for controlled studies. A logging mode provides reproducible timelines of allocations and migrations to aid analysis. We implement SHAMBLES on a commodity Linux system with HBM and DDR exposed as NUMA nodes and evaluate it with the HPCG, DGEMM benchmarks and Himeno stencil mini-app. Our design and methodology show how transparent, policy-driven migration can respond to changing access locality and concentrate hot data in HBM without developer intervention, offering a practical path to performance portability on tiered memory. Results from HPCG show that we can maintain up to 93.75% of the all-in-HBM baseline performance, while keeping only 40% of the problem size in the HBM. DGEMM experiments show that dynamic policies in SHAMBLES sustain up to 99% of the all-in-HBM performance, while keeping only one third of the DGEMM matrix footprint in HBM. For Himeno, SHAMBLES shows that fast-tier selection must be both workload-aware and size-aware: with a 50% fast-tier budget, it can outperform fixed all-in-HBM and all-in-DDR placements for the L size, while the XL size shifts back toward HBM.

♻ ☆ SIGMA: A Versatile Streaming Graph Partitioner for Vertex- and Edge-Balanced Distributed GNN Training
Barbara Hoffmann, Shai Dorian Peretz, Adil Chhabra, Ahmet Kadir Yalcinkaya, Ruben Mayer, Christian Schulz
Distributed Graph Neural Network (GNN) training depends critically on how the underlying graph is partitioned across compute resources. Existing graph partitioners focus either on vertex partitioning or edge partitioning and typically optimize only a single communication objective (edge cut vertex cut) under a single balance constraint (vertex balance edge balance). We present SIGMA (Streaming Integrated Graph Partitioning with Multi-objective Awareness), a versatile streaming graph partitioner that supports both vertex and edge partitioning within a unified multi-objective, multi-constraint framework. Depending on the target distributed GNN system, SIGMA can be configured for edge-cut-oriented vertex partitioning or vertex-cut-oriented edge partitioning while simultaneously accounting for vertex and edge balancing. A clustering-based preprocessing stage incorporates global graph structure to improve partition quality while preserving the efficiency and scalability advantages of streaming partitioning. We evaluate SIGMA on six benchmark graphs spanning diverse domains and scales using two distributed GNN training systems: DistGNN (edge-partitioned) and DistDGL (vertex-partitioned). Across both settings, SIGMA consistently achieves strong performance, showing its ability to navigate complex trade-offs between partition quality, training efficiency, and memory consumption, frequently outperforming established streaming approaches and delivering competitive results against high-quality in-memory partitioners, with particularly strong results in edge-partitioned GNN training. These results demonstrate that a unified streaming partitioner can effectively address the communication, compute, and memory challenges of distributed GNN training across fundamentally different system architectures.
♻ ☆ Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
Grigory Begunov, Alexander Tyurin
Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.
♻ ☆ Bitcoin-IPC: Scaling Bitcoin with a Network of Proof-of-Stake Subnets
Orestis Alpos, Jakov Mitrovski, Themis Papameletiou, Nikola Ristić, Dionysis Zindros, Marko Vukolić
Despite holding over $1.7T in value, Bitcoin scales poorly: Layer-1 (L1) processes only a few transactions per second, and Layer-2 (L2) solutions suffer from operational and liquidity fragmentation that requires external bridges for cross-chain connectivity. We present Bitcoin-IPC, a protocol that horizontally scales Bitcoin via permissionless, interconnected, programmable Proof-of-Stake L2 subnets staked in L1 BTC. Subnets leverage Bitcoin L1 for interconnectivity, settlement, and security, including Sybil protection, equivocating validator slashing, unilateral exit for honest stake, long-range attack protection, and compromised subnet firewalling. Bitcoin-IPC cross-subnet transfers involve only source/destination subnet validators and L1, with no external bridges or per-path liquidity lock-up. Embedded and batched in Bitcoin's witness mechanism, cross-subnet settlements can approach 6 vB per transfer, 23x less than a native L1 payment. Filling Bitcoin blocks with such batches corresponds to L1 monetary throughput of about 273 transfers per second, without modifying Bitcoin.
♻ ☆ PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors
