Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client's feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. When feature geometry and decision rules co-vary, the PH partition recovers the latent client groups, including differences a linear-subspace descriptor misses, and pTopoFL is competitive with the strongest clustered baselines; on the real federation it lowers the test log-loss of FedAvg from 0.463 to 0.438, on par with the best personalised methods. When heterogeneity is invisible in feature geometry, it offers no advantage over FedAvg. pTopoFL transmits model parameters and is no more private than FedAvg; we give a record-level differential-privacy accounting and show that privatising the descriptor destroys the partition. Code reproduces every number.

♻ ☆ Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
Anton Altenbernd, Dylan Everingham, Philipp Wiesner, Odej Kao
Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths. Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated linear layers in dense LLMs, while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting linear layers in dense LLMs, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.
♻ ☆ ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models

However, this approach fails to address critical memory constraints and suffers from inherently coarse balancing granularity. In this paper, we propose Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism (HPP), a novel approach enabling efficient and fine-grained data balance across heterogeneous pipelines. To address HPP's key challenges, prohibitive search overhead for optimal configurations and high communication overhead from asymmetric All-Reduce, we design the ETH training system. ETH employs a hierarchical workload balance framework that jointly optimizes balance across heterogeneous pipelines and within individual pipeline stages. To mitigate asymmetric communication costs, ETH implements block-wise gradient aggregation. Furthermore, it integrates specialized optimizations that dramatically reduce HPP configuration search overhead. Evaluations demonstrate ETH achieves up to 2x training speedup while reducing configuration generation overhead by up to 56x compared to state-of-the-art systems. The code is available at https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH.

☆ StreamAhead: Real-Time Streaming Video Question Answering via Adaptive Precomputation
Haoyang Fan, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.

In contrast, Plumtree's own link optimization and shorter repair timeouts, which also exploit non-tree links, rewire the shared tree and increase latency as broadcast sources change; the latency of exuding is nearly unaffected.

In an adversarial uniform-emission benchmark, the RDMA backend sustains $>97\%$ weak-scaling and $>88\%$ strong-scaling efficiency up to 13,440~cores (112~cores per network adapter), with $1.14$-$1.27\times$ speedups over the two-sided alternative. In a Hohlraum IMC benchmark at 4480 ranks, it is $1.41\times$ faster because MPI progress overhead is reduced by $6.1\times$. By decoupling communication from physics models and mesh representations, STORM removes a barrier to scaling Monte Carlo transport in astrophysical multiphysics codes, enabling coupled radiation-hydrodynamics with energy- and angle-resolved photon or neutrino transport on dynamically evolving meshes at scale.

Large language model (LLM) agents face a structural tension: cloud agents provide strong reasoning but expose user data, while on-device agents preserve privacy at the cost of overall capability. Existing device-cloud designs treat this boundary as a compute split rather than a trust boundary suited to agentic workloads, and existing sanitizers force a choice between policy flexibility and the structural fidelity tool calls require. In this work, we develop PAAC, a privacy-aware agentic framework that aligns planner--executor decomposition with the device-cloud boundary so that role specialization itself becomes the privacy mechanism. The cloud agent reasons over typed placeholder tokens that preserve each sensitive value's reasoning role while discarding its content, while the on-device agent identifies sensitive spans and distills each step's execution outcome into compact key findings. Sanitization confines the on-device LLM to proposing which spans to mask, while a deterministic registry performs all substitution and reversal, keeping actions directly executable on device. On three agentic benchmarks under strict privacy settings, PAAC dominates the Pareto frontier of privacy and accuracy, improving average accuracy by 15-36\% and reducing average leakage by 2-6$\times$ over state-of-the-art device-cloud baselines, with the largest margins on privacy targets outside fixed entity taxonomies. We find consistent improvements on 17 additional benchmarks spanning 10 domains, including math, science, and finance.

Agnieszka M. Łupińska, Serban D. Porumbescu, John D. Owens
We describe a GPU-resident runtime system, HEL, built on stateful services that persist throughout the lifespan of a user application. A HEL programmer expresses a workload as an application that spawns coroutine-like tasks, which are then scheduled and run by the HEL runtime. Yu Wang, Zhu Wang, Ning Hu, Yifan Guo, Xiu Ma, Bin Guo, Zhiwen Yu
Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.

☆ Low-Bit Distributed Constrained Optimization with Application to Optimal Scheduling and Allocation
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian, Sergio Pequito
This paper proposes a distributed resource allocation algorithm in which each agent communicates only the sign of its local cost gradient, a single bit per directed link per iteration. The algorithm is based on Laplacian-gradient dynamics and preserves the equality (demand) constraint at every iterate, guaranteeing anytime feasibility irrespective of termination time. First, we provide a complete Lyapunov-based convergence analysis for the fixed-step-size regime: the iterates are shown to enter, in at most O(1/\varepsilon^2) iterations, a neighborhood of the optimizer whose radius scales as O(τ) in the decision variable and O(τ^2) in the cost residual, where $τ$ is the step-size. Crucially, the step-size bound is a time-invariant network constant (depending only on the graph Laplacian spectrum and the cost curvature bounds), so no adaptive tuning is required. Second, we characterize the invariant set under B-connected, weight-balanced digraphs, strictly weaker than the all-time connectivity and doubly-stochastic weights assumed in most prior work, and show that any odd, sign-preserving nonlinearity yields the same invariant-set and descent structure, with the single-bit protocol being the extreme communication-minimizing instance of a broader nonlinear class. Third, we address local box constraints via smooth penalty relaxation and quantify explicitly how the penalty weight interacts with the step-size bound and the optimality gap. Simulations on economic dispatch (1000 generators) and CPU scheduling (500 servers) demonstrate that the single-bit protocol achieves 5-60 times reduction in total communication cost relative to multi-bit baselines, at the price of a tunable and explicitly bounded optimality gap. A diminishing step-size schedule is shown empirically to eliminate this gap; its formal convergence analysis is identified as an open problem.

♻ ☆ NosRacer: Dynamic Detection of Race Conditions in On-Device Network Operating Systems ATC 2026
Runze Wu, Jingbo Zhai, Shanming Ping, Lingzhi Ouyang, Hua Duan, Qin Zou, Chengcheng Huang, Bingshe Liu, Xudong Lang, Xiaoxing Ma, Yu Huang
Commercial on-device network operating systems (NOSes) run the complex control planes of production routers and switches, where configuration update tasks are executed by multiple loosely coupled components through asynchronous message passing. Such executions are prone to race conditions: the same ordered input commands may produce different outcomes when messages are delivered in different orders. The race conditions are difficult to expose because they often manifest only as subtle, delayed malfunctions. Existing static analysis techniques lack scalability and precision for large-scale industrial NOSes, while dynamic ones incur substantial system-execution cost when attempting to cover the space of asynchronous message interleavings. To address the challenges above, we present NosRacer, a dynamic analysis framework for race condition detection in industrial-grade on-device NOSes. NosRacer uses a two-phase design. The concentration phase reduces analysis scope by leveraging the locality of configuration update tasks. Race condition detection is then limited to a small subset of involved components and crucial state variables, thereby reducing the detection cost. The perturbation phase proactively perturbs message asynchrony to increase the likelihood of executions with race-condition-exposing message interleavings. It keeps perturbation practical by grouping compatible perturbations for parallel execution and adaptively strengthening perturbations. We implement NosRacer in a commercial, actively developed NOS. NosRacer is integrated into the existing testing factory and used to detect race conditions in 5 key control-plane components. NosRacer achieves 66% precision and detects 21 race conditions confirmed by developers as severe bugs, while keeping the detection overhead below 10%.

♻ ☆ Domain Extension of Lock-Freedom and Wait-Freedom for Group Computations
Raaghav Ravishankar, Sandeep Kulkarni, Sathya Peri, Gokarna Sharma, Manaswini Piduguralla, Yashi Rastogi
A domain extension of a definition refers to broadening the scope of a definition so that it applies to a larger set of cases than originally specified. The notion of lock-free and wait-free computation is designed for the domain of tasks that are completed by a single thread (in competition with other threads). The goal of this paper is to extend the definition of lock-freedom and wait-freedom to group-computations (denoted by gl-freedom and gw-freedom) that require that the task at hand must be completed by a collaboration between multiple threads. When extending a definition, certain constraints must be respected: the new domain must remain logically consistent with the original meaning, the extension should not introduce contradictions or ambiguities, and it must preserve the essential properties that make the definition valid and useful. We demonstrate this by showing that our extended definition is consistent with the original definition when the group consists of a single thread. We note that extension allows us to characterize programs in a new domain (distributed computing, NUMA computation systems, systems with private data for different threads, etc.) instead of relegating them to be in the same category (deadlock/livelock-free) without regard to the actual properties of that program. We also illustrate this definition with various examples.

Sub-model federated learning allows clients with limited memory and compute to join training by optimising width-reduced slices of a shared global network. Established schemes such as HeteroFL and FjORD size these slices from device resources alone, and a growing line of adaptive methods proposes to also enlarge the slices of clients whose data deviate most from the population, inferring that deviation from the model updates the server already receives. This paper puts that design pattern to a controlled test. We construct HAS-FL, a representative heterogeneity-aware allocation framework that isolates this inference step, and evaluate it on CIFAR-10, EMNIST and the naturally partitioned Shakespeare corpus. We find that the inference step fails: divergence between local and global updates tracks the width of each client's sub-model, with a strong negative correlation in every image run, and carries little or no information about ground-truth label skew once width is held fixed. We also identify a separate failure of capped allocation: weights that no client trains remain at their random initial values yet still enter every forward pass, driving accuracy close to chance on the 62-class EMNIST task; guaranteeing that every parameter is trained by at least one client removes this failure. Finally, a random allocation with the same average budget matches the adaptive policy on the image tasks and surpasses it on text. The gains attributed to adaptive allocation therefore come from capacity budgeting and parameter coverage rather than heterogeneity estimation, and we recommend capacity-stratified validation and matched-budget random baselines as standard practice.

RDMA networking enables low-latency, high-bandwidth communication on large systems. Despite its adoption, however, observability is lacking. Existing tools target specific communication libraries or only report aggregated data, missing per-operation behavior. ☆ Empirical Analysis of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs
Claudiu-Nicu Bărbieru, Corentin Libert, Peterson Yuhala, Andrei Arusoaie, Matthieu Bettinger, Oana-Otilia Captarencu, Pascal Felber, Emanuel Onica, Etienne Rivière, Valerio Schiavoni
Layer 2 (L2) rollups have become the dominant scaling solution in Ethereum. At the core of these systems lies the rollup sequencer, a component that orders, executes, and submits L2 transaction blocks to the main Ethereum blockchain. The centralization of this sequencer introduces security risks, including censorship and malicious manipulation of transactions to extract maximum extractable value (MEV). Trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide strong hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity guarantees for code and data. TEEs are strong candidates for strengthening security and ensuring verifiable neutrality in rollup sequencer operations, but multiple TEE-based designs are possible, offering different trade-offs among modularity, performance, and security guarantees. Among them, the separation of proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services is a strong contender against the monolithic approach that bundles all sequencer logic. Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers. This work addresses this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of TEE-enabled rollup designs under both PBS and monolithic sequencer models. Our experimental evaluations show that the impact of TEEs on rollup performance is small and that PBS does not significantly amplify it. We also show that PBS can lead to significant performance improvements by enabling more specialized, efficient builder logic implementations.

Evaluation shows that KVCompass achieves $1.3-14\times$ lower P99 TTFT than the baselines, up to $3.7\times$ lower P99 end-to-end latency, up to $4.7\times$ the throughput, and a peak load factor within 2% of the Oracle floor.

We study alternation hierarchies for distributed decision in anonymous networks with constant-size certificates. A prover and a disprover alternately assign certificates to nodes over a constant number of rounds, after which each node decides whether to accept based on its own input and the certificates observed in its neighborhood. An instance is accepted if all nodes accept. Unlike previous work on distributed alternation hierarchies, which considered restricted local computation (Reiter, PODC 2024) or logarithmic-size certificates (Feuilloley et al., ICALP 2016), we focus on constant-size certificates and the role of neighborhood information in determining expressive power. We consider three models: SET, where nodes observe only the set of certificate sequences of their neighbors; MULTISET, where multiplicities are also visible; and PORTS, where neighbors can additionally be distinguished by local port numbers. We establish that SET is strictly weaker than MULTISET, which is in turn strictly weaker than PORTS, and that all three alternation hierarchies are strict at every level. Despite their severe restrictions, these models are remarkably expressive: LEADER belongs to the third level of SET. Our main characterization shows that, over finite input alphabets, SET coincides exactly with monadic second-order logic (MSO$_1$). Moreover, every language definable in counting monadic second-order logic (CMSO$_1$) belongs to PORTS, while MULTISET already contains languages that are not CMSO$_1$-definable. Nevertheless, this expressive power has fundamental limitations. PORTS does not capture MSO$_2$: neither Hamiltonicity nor the existence of a perfect matching belongs to PORTS. Furthermore, over unbounded input alphabets, PORTS cannot verify that every node has been given the correct network size.
♻ ☆ All-out Attack: Optimal Block Withholding Under Pay-Per-Share Scheme
Mustafa Doger, Sennur Ulukus
Classical Block Withholding (BWH) attacks have been extensively studied in block-dependent reward schemes, where pool members are compensated upon a block discovery within the pool. However, most contemporary mining pools operate under share-based schemes, wherein participants are paid immediately upon submission of valid shares. In this paper, we analyze BWH under Pay-Per-Share (PPS) for Nakamoto-style blockchains and prove that these mechanisms are not incentive compatible, contrary to conclusions drawn under fixed difficulty in prior literature. Under PPS, the optimal strategy for a BWH attacker is the All-out Attack (AoA): the adversary allocates its entire hashpower toward the victim pool, submitting only partial Proof-of-Work shares (pPoW) while withholding all valid blocks, i.e., full Proof-of-Work (fPoW). Prior to the first difficulty adjustment, the adversary incurs negligible loss from withheld fPoWs. After the adjustment reduces block difficulty, the adversary either generates more pPoWs per unit time when the pPoW difficulty is reduced accordingly or, if the pPoW difficulty is held fixed, earns a higher reward per share. In both cases, it achieves a post-adjustment reward rate of $\fracα{1-α}$ per target epoch, compared with the honest baseline rate of $α$. Remarkably, this gain matches the theoretical upper bound achieved by optimal selfish mining in Nakamoto consensus under perfect network influence. The results further indicate that BWH is substantially more profitable under PPS than under mainstream block-dependent payout schemes, even when compared with advanced BWH variants. Honest miners benefit at the same rate as the adversary per unit hashpower, while the victim pool operator bears all losses, paying out-of-pocket for pPoW submissions without receiving fPoW compensation in return.

We focus on the {\em away model}, in which the target moves {\em away} from the origin with speed $v<1$. For each setting, we derive upper bounds on the competitive ratio and for some cases, we derive the lower bound. Our results highlight how the number of rays and the communication model influence the competitive ratio.

For fixed per-walk random inputs, the ordering preserves the multiset of sampled walks while improving locality during neighbor access. We study a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics solver and propose memory layout strategies for host-side particle data that are particularly well-suited to GPU-offloading. Specifically, we advocate splitting classic array-of-struct data structures into a struct-of-arrays-of-structs arrangement, in which each logical struct decomposes into substructs determined by kernel read/write access patterns and attribute types. Splitting a monolithic particle struct into several bespoke, finer-grained structs can reduce the time required to pack data to and from buffers by ~20%-40%, lowering total time spent on GPU-offloading by ~12%-25%.
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Accepted and presented in PPAM 2026 conference
♻ ☆ Differential Refresh of Materialized Derived State: From a Single-Age Equivalence Limit to an Optimal Per-Partition Allocation, with a Real-System Validation on Materialized Views
Amit Rajula
Materialized views, cached aggregates, and trained models are all derived state: query results precomputed from base relations that begin to age the instant they are built, because the data they summarize keeps changing. A common way to keep such state fresh is to replace a fixed recompute cadence with an adaptive trigger -- a weighted staleness score that recomputes when accumulated base-data change crosses a threshold. We show this is the wrong lever and identify the right one. First, an equivalence limit: any refresh trigger that is a static, strictly monotone function of a single shared age of a globally-recomputed artifact is operationally equivalent to a calibrated periodic timer, so a global weighted staleness budget cannot schedule a recompute that a uniform timer could not. The escape is to enlarge the state: refresh partitions (the groups of a GROUP BY, per-tenant views, or data segments) differentially, each on its own schedule. We solve the resulting budget-allocation problem: the optimal per-partition recompute rate is proportional to the square root of partition risk sqrt(w_j*lambda_j), and the policy never costs more than the uniform timer, beating it by a closed-form Cauchy-Schwarz "price of uniformity" that grows with heterogeneity. We validate three ways -- analytic, discrete-event simulation, and a real relational engine (SQLite) maintaining materialized GROUP BY views with real SQL and wall-clock timing -- where the policy lowers realized weighted staleness by 14-15% at matched recompute count, winning on every run, while a naive per-partition exposure threshold does not reliably help. The rule for any periodically-recomputed derived state: a global staleness score is a timer in disguise; the leverage is differential refresh allocated by the square root of partition risk.
♻ ☆ Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
Bernhard Klein, Falk Selker, Hendrik Borras, Sophie Steger, Franz Pernkopf, Holger Fröning
Machine learning models perform well across domains such as diagnostics, weather forecasting, NLP, and autonomous driving, but their limited uncertainty handling restricts use in safety-critical settings. Traditional neural networks often fail to detect out-of-domain (OOD) data and may output confident yet incorrect predictions. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address this by providing probabilistic estimates, but incur high computational cost because predictions require sampling weight distributions and multiple forward passes. The Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) offers a highly efficient approximation to Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI) by assuming Gaussian-distributed weights and activations, enabling fully analytic uncertainty propagation and replacing sampling with a single deterministic forward pass. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compiling, optimizing, and deploying PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. Using the TVM deep learning compiler, we implement a dedicated library of Gaussian-propagating operators for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks, combined with manual and automated tuning strategies. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency, achieving speedups of up to 4200x for small mini-batches. PFP-BNNs match SVI-BNNs on Dirty-MNIST in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and OOD detection while greatly reducing compute cost. These results highlight the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation to enable efficient BNN deployment on resource-constrained systems.
comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization (TACO)
♻ ☆ Optimistic, Signature-Free Reliable Broadcast and Its Applications
Nibesh Shrestha, Qianyu Yu, Aniket Kate, Giuliano Losa, Kartik Nayak, Xuechao Wang
Reliable broadcast (RBC) is a key primitive in fault-tolerant distributed systems, and improving its efficiency can benefit a wide range of applications. This work focuses on signature-free RBC protocols, which are particularly attractive due to their computational efficiency. Existing protocols in this setting incur an optimal 3 steps to reach a decision while tolerating up to $f < n/3$ Byzantine faults, where $n$ is the number of parties. In this work, we propose an optimistic RBC protocol that maintains the $f < n/3$ fault tolerance but achieves termination in just 2 steps under certain optimistic conditions--when at least $\lceil \frac{n+2f-2}{2} \rceil$ non-broadcaster parties behave honestly. We also prove a matching lower bound on the number of honest parties required for 2-step termination. We show that our latency-reduction technique generalizes beyond RBC and applies to other primitives such as asynchronous verifiable secret sharing (AVSS) and asynchronous verifiable information dispersal (AVID), enabling them to complete in 2 steps under similar optimistic conditions. To highlight the practical impact of our RBC protocol, we integrate it into Sailfish++, a new signature-free, post-quantum secure DAG-based Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus protocol. Under optimistic conditions, this protocol achieves a commit latency of 3 steps--matching the performance of the best signature-based protocols. Our experimental evaluation shows that our protocol significantly outperforms existing post-quantum secure and signature-based protocols, even on machines with limited CPU resources. In contrast, signature-based protocols require high CPU capacity to achieve comparable performance. We have open-sourced our Rust implementation of Sailfish++ to facilitate reproducible results.
comment: Updated artifact citation to the Zenodo version including the Ivy and Isabelle proofs
♻ ☆ Federated k-Core Decomposition: A Secure Distributed Approach
Bin Guo, Emil Sekerinski, Lingyang Chu
As one of the most well-studied cohesive subgraph models, the $k$-core is widely used to find graph nodes that are ``central'' or ``important'' in many applications, such as biological networks, social networks, ecological networks, and financial networks. For Decentralized Online Social Networks (DOSNs), where each vertex is a client as a single computing unit, distributed k-core decomposition algorithms have already been proposed. However, current distributed approaches fail to adequately protect privacy and security. In today's data-driven world, data privacy and security have attracted more and more attention, e.g., DOSNs are proposed to protect privacy by storing user information locally without using a single centralized server. In this work, we are the first to propose the secure version of the distributed $k$-core decomposition.
